newsitem.title: USA: Birth control options limited for many women: study.
newsitem.headline: Birth control options limited for many women: study.

text.p: Millions of women around the world lack access to birth control, which remains an obstacle to improving women's health, a study said on Sunday.

"Contraceptive choice is fundamental to women's health and represents not only a chance to plan their families but to plan their lives," said Shanti Conly, director of policy research for Population Action International.

The Washington-based group said progress has been made in developing countries during the past 15 years, but large gaps remain. Too many women still have poor access to contraception and few choices about what methods are available for avoiding unwanted pregnancies, it said.

The abortion rate, however, dropped in countries where access to contraception improved such as Chile, Colombia, Hungary and South Korea, the study found. The abortion rate and the annual number of abortions has also dropped in Russia, Kazakstan and Ukraine, it said.

The group said women need to be able to choose from a number of different options because no one method is appropriate for all couples. In some countries sterilization is relatively easy to obtain, but access to reversible contraceptives is limited. Elsewhere the reverse is true.

More than 100 million married women around the world have an unmet need for contraception, the study said. In some African countries, one out of three women has an unmet need for family planning and they often outnumber those who do use contraception.
In general, poorer developing countries have worse contraception access than richer ones, but there are exceptions, shaped by cultural and governmental factors.

For instance, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are very poor but government support for family planning is strong, while Saudi Arabia and Argentina are far richer, but government policies restrict access to contraception, Conly said.
